item.title: Webhooks Arrive Out of Order: How My Scheduler Killed Live Builds
item.description: The scheduler in ephemerd is event-driven. GitHub sends a workflow_job webhook when a job is queued, when it starts and when it completes. ephemerd creates and destroys runners to match. For a while that worked well enough that I stopped thinking about it. Then a docker-build job failed with “The self-hosted runner lost communication with the server”. I pulled the node’s journal. ephemerd had destroyed that runner itself, on purpose, while it was running the build.

item.title: Bind Mounts Across Mount Namespaces: Four PRs and a Container Escape
item.description: GitHub Actions has a container: key that runs a job’s steps inside an image of your choosing. It’s popular because it gives you a reproducible toolchain without building a custom runner image. On a self-hosted runner it works by having the runner drive Docker. On ephemerd, “Docker” is a shim that speaks the Docker API and creates containers in containerd. Getting bind mounts right through that shim took four PRs in a week. A couple of months later the version that worked turned out to be an escape.

item.title: shipmates Short Ones: 8 Minutes Extracting Go, and Three Voice-Loop Bugs
item.description:
A few shipmates bugs don’t need a whole post each. They were too good to leave in commit messages, though.

setup-go spends 8 minutes extracting Go on Windows CI

shipmates CI runs on my own ephemerd runners. On Windows those jobs run inside a Hyper-V utility VM. The windows-x64 leg kept timing out in actions/setup-go. Here’s the log from PR #48:

20:58:46  Setup go version spec 1.26.6
20:58:46  Attempting to download 1.26.6...     <- tool-cache MISS
20:58:48  Acquiring 1.26.6 from ...zip
20:58:53  Extracting Go...
21:06:46  ERROR: The action 'Run actions/setup-go@v5' has timed out after 8 minutes

Seven seconds from the start of the step to Extracting Go.... Then almost eight minutes extracting until the step timeout killed it.

item.title: ephemerd: One Daemon, a Fresh Runner Per Job, Every OS
item.description: I have CI that needs Linux amd64, Linux arm64, Windows and macOS. GitHub-hosted runners for all four get expensive fast, especially the arm64 and Mac minutes. Self-hosted runners fix the bill and create a different problem. A stock actions/runner on a box you own runs whatever the workflow says. It keeps whatever the last job left behind. And it’s one fork PR away from somebody running code on your LAN.

item.title: Escaping WSL: Booting My Own Linux VM Through Hyper-V's HCS API
item.description:
I’ve been building ephemerd, a daemon that runs self-hosted GitHub Actions runners with a fresh environment per job. On a Windows host, Windows jobs run in Hyper-V isolated containers. Linux jobs still need a Linux kernel from somewhere. The obvious answer on Windows in 2026 is WSL2, and that’s what I used first. It worked great from my terminal and fell over the moment ephemerd became a real Windows service.

WSL2 doesn’t do LocalSystem

A Windows service that wants to create containers and Hyper-V VMs runs as LocalSystem. WSL2 doesn’t support that context at all. You get WSL_E_LOCAL_SYSTEM_NOT_SUPPORTED and that’s the end of the conversation. There’s no flag for it. WSL is a per-user feature and a service account isn’t a user.
